transcript.text: LG FWV917BTSE keeps stopping with tE on the screen during the 60 wash. Turned it off and on, worked once, now it's back. Whats wrong with it?

On LG washing machines and washer-dryers, tE is generally a heating/temperature error. The machine checks how fast the water warms up and what the temperature sensor reports. If the reading is missing, implausible, or the water isn't warming as expected, it stops. That fits it happening on a 60°C wash. A reset that works once and then fails again usually points to a component that's failing or making intermittent contact, not a one-off glitch. 1. The wash temperature sensor (NTC thermistor) or its plug. This is the commonest cause of a temperature error that comes and goes.
2. The wash heater element. If it has failed, the water never warms and the machine times out with an error.
3. A loose or corroded connector on the heater/sensor wiring, or much less often the control board. 1. Run a cold or 30°C wash. If it finishes cleanly, that backs up a heating-side fault rather than a general control problem.
2. Run the 60°C wash and touch the door glass after about 20 minutes. If the glass and water are clearly warm before the error, the heater is working and the temperature sensor becomes the prime suspect. If it's stone cold, the heater element (or its wiring) is more likely.
3. Notice whether the house electrics ever trip when it errors. That would point firmly at the heater element leaking to earth. If so, stop using it until it's checked. If you're confident with a multimeter, the heater and sensor can be resistance-tested with the machine unplugged. That means removing a panel to reach them, so many people hand this part to an engineer. Until it's sorted, cold and low-temperature washes should still work, though it's best not to rely on it. So: does a cold or 30° wash complete OK, and does the glass get warm on the 60° wash before it stops?
Cold and 30 washes finish fine (20 and 30 anyway). On the 60 the door glass stays cold, and no trips or burning smells either.

That narrows it down well. Washes at 20 and 30 finish fine, so the general control side is working. On the 60, the glass stays cold, so the water isn't being heated at all, and the machine gives up with tE when the temperature doesn't rise. 1. Wash heater element: the most likely cause. An element that has gone open circuit produces no heat at all. It won't trip the electrics, because only a heater leaking to earth does that. 2. Heater wiring or connector: a loose, corroded or heat-discoloured terminal on the element can give exactly this on-off behaviour.
3. Temperature sensor (NTC): less likely now. A cold-glass result usually means no heat, not a misread. Still, a sensor reading open or nonsense can stop the board switching the heater on. I'd put it at fairly confident on the heating side, with the element the most likely part. 1. Switch off at the wall and unplug, and leave it a while if it has just run.
2. On many front-loaders the heater is reached by removing the back panel. It sits at the bottom of the tub with two terminals and the small temperature sensor plugged in nearby.
3. Before testing, look at the connectors. If one is loose, burnt or green with corrosion, that is the likely culprit.
4. Pull the two spade connectors off the element and measure across the terminals. A UK element typically reads somewhere around 20–30 ohms. If it reads open circuit (no reading), the element has failed. If it reads within that range, the element is probably fine, and the wiring or the temperature sensor becomes the suspect. If you'd rather not take the panel off, this is a straightforward job for an engineer. The heater is usually a reasonably priced part on a machine like this, so a repair is normally well worth doing. In the meantime it's fine to keep using 20–30°C washes. Are you comfortable doing a multimeter resistance test on the heater with the machine unplugged, or would you rather hand this to an engineer?

Not doing that myself, I've no multimeter and I'm not taking the back off or tipping it with my back. It's in a fitted space under the worktop too. Is it worth getting an engineer in for a 3 year old machine, and would it be the heater or the sensor?

[Heading: Likely cause: heater element]
Yes, on a 3-year-old LG it's normally well worth getting an engineer in. The machine is young, the 20 and 30°C washes run fine so the rest of it is working, and a heater fault is usually one of the cheaper repairs. It's a fraction of the cost of a replacement machine. Heater or sensor: my money is on the heater element, but I'm fairly sure rather than certain. The glass stays stone cold on a 60°C wash, which means no heat is being made at all. That's what a dead element does. A faulty sensor more often gives the wrong temperature or an on-off fault than complete cold. An engineer can test the element, the sensor and the plugs in a few minutes once the back is off, so you'd only pay for the part that's actually faulty. I couldn't confirm the exact heater part for the FWV917BTSE. Let the engineer or LG's own spares service match it to your model number, rather than buying one yourself on a guess. 1. Check whether you have any cover. That could be a retailer extended warranty, a product-protection plan, or appliance cover on your home insurance. At 3 years, it may also be worth asking the retailer whether this counts as a premature fault. Results vary, so it's not guaranteed.
2. Give the engineer the details up front: tE code on 60°C washes only, glass stays cold, 20/30°C washes finish fine, no trips or burning smell. They can then bring a likely heater with them.
3. Mention that it's built in under the worktop, and clear the space in front so they can slide it out. Pulling it out is part of their job, so you won't need to move it. Until then, 20–30°C washes are fine to keep using. If it ever starts tripping the electrics or smells of burning, stop using it.
